title: Replacing half of faculty-led examination-skills teaching with near-peer sessions: cost and effect
subtitle: Cost-effectiveness analysis for a medical school decision
statement: The clinical skills centre is asked to replace four of the eight faculty-led examination-skills sessions for second-year students with near-peer sessions taught by trained final-year students. The school needs to know what the change would cost and whether first-attempt pass rates on the OSCE examination-skills stations would be maintained, when existing comparisons are distorted because students chose whether to attend near-peer sessions.
whoAffected: About 180 second-year students per year, final-year near-peer tutors, faculty clinicians paid at sessional rates, and the school's budget holders.
whatHurts: Faculty sessions are hard to book and expensive; replacing them without evidence could lower examination performance, while keeping them may waste scarce clinician time.
currentPractice: Eight faculty-led sessions for all second-years, plus optional near-peer sessions since 2024.
whyNow: The dean wants a decision for next year's timetable, and four years of station scores and two years of attendance registers are available.
constraints: No funding. Existing data only, plus about 4 hours per week of the director's and an education fellow's time from October 2026 to May 2027. Student data may be used only in de-identified form under the school's education data policy.
patientCenteredGoal: Future patients are examined competently by graduates, whichever teaching format is used.
summary: Problem framed as a cost-effectiveness question about a teaching change, with self-selection as the main threat.
